statement: The FRTB standardized approach includes a risk charge calculated with a sensitivities-based method.
explanation: The FRTB standardized capital charge is the sum of a sensitivities-based risk charge, a default risk charge and a residual risk add-on.
originalText: A risk charge calculated using a risk sensitivity approach

statement: The FRTB standardized approach includes a residual risk add-on.
explanation: The residual risk add-on captures exotic and other risks not covered by the sensitivities-based method; it is one of the three components of the standardized charge.
originalText: A residual risk add‑on

statement: The FRTB standardized approach includes a default risk charge.
explanation: The default risk charge, which captures jump-to-default risk, is one of the three components of the FRTB standardized charge.
originalText: A default risk charge

statement: The FRTB standardized approach includes an insolvency risk charge as one of its components.
explanation: The standardized charge has exactly three components: the sensitivities-based risk charge, the default risk charge and the residual risk add-on. There is no insolvency risk charge.
originalText: Insolvency risk charge

statement: Under the FRTB, a liquidity horizon is the time required to sell a security in a stressed market without materially affecting market prices.
explanation: A liquidity horizon is the period, assessed in stressed market conditions, that it takes to exit a risk factor exposure without materially moving the market. Longer horizons (10 to 120 days) imply larger capital.
originalText: The time required to sell a security in a stressed market, without materially affecting market prices

statement: Under the FRTB, a liquidity horizon is the time taken to find a willing buyer for a security or commodity.
explanation: Finding a buyer is only part of an exit. The liquidity horizon is the time needed to complete the sale or hedge in stressed conditions without materially affecting prices.
originalText: The time taken to find a willing buyer for a security or commodity

statement: Under the FRTB, a liquidity horizon is the time taken to execute a sale that guarantees a minimum level of profit.
explanation: A liquidity horizon concerns how long it takes to exit an exposure in stressed markets without moving prices. It has nothing to do with guaranteeing a profit.
originalText: The time taken to successfully execute a sale transaction that guarantees a minimum level of profit

statement: Under the FRTB, a liquidity horizon is the time it takes to buy a security or commodity.
explanation: The liquidity horizon concerns exiting or hedging an existing exposure in stressed markets, not buying a position.
originalText: The time it takes to buy a security or commodity

statement: In the FRTB liquidity-adjusted expected shortfall, ES$_{j}$ is the ES from a 10-day shock to liquidity-horizon categories j through 5 only, each ES$_{j}$ (j ≥ 2) is scaled by $\sqrt{(LH_{j} - LH_{j-1})/10}$, and total ES is the square root of the sum of the squared terms because the horizons are treated as independent.
explanation: The cascade removes lower-horizon categories step by step and scales each incremental horizon by the square-root rule. Because shocks in different horizon buckets are assumed independent, the pieces are aggregated in quadrature.
originalText: ES$_{j}$ is the ES from a 10‑day shock to categories j through 5 only, holding categories 1 to j‑1 constant. Each ES$_{j}$ (j ≥ 2) is scaled by $\sqrt{(LH_{j} - LH_{j-1})/10}$, and total ES is the square root of the sum of the squared terms, reflecting independence across horizons.

statement: In the FRTB liquidity-adjusted expected shortfall, the five cascade terms are added together in a simple sum because changes in the risk factor groups are assumed perfectly correlated.
explanation: The FRTB formula assumes the horizon buckets are independent and combines the cascade terms as the square root of the sum of squares, not as a simple sum.
originalText: ES$_{j}$ is the ES from a 10‑day shock to categories j through 5 only, scaled by $\sqrt{(LH_{j} - LH_{j-1})/10}$, but total ES is the simple sum of the five terms because variable changes are assumed perfectly correlated, the most conservative assumption.

statement: In the FRTB liquidity-adjusted expected shortfall, each cascade term ES$_{j}$ is scaled by $\sqrt{LH_{j}/10}$, using the full liquidity horizon rather than the incremental horizon.
explanation: Each term is scaled by $\sqrt{(LH_{j} - LH_{j-1})/10}$, the incremental horizon. Using the full horizon would double count time already covered by the lower-numbered ES terms.
originalText: ES$_{j}$ is the ES from a 10‑day shock to categories j through 5 only, but each is scaled by $\sqrt{LH_{j}/10}$ (the full horizon), and total ES is the square root of the sum of the squared terms.
correction: In the FRTB liquidity-adjusted expected shortfall, each cascade term ES$_{j}$ is scaled by $\sqrt{(LH_{j} - LH_{j-1})/10}$, using the incremental liquidity horizon rather than the full horizon.

changes.from: using the full liquidity horizon rather than the incremental horizon
changes.to: using the incremental liquidity horizon rather than the full horizon

statement: The FRTB computes liquidity-adjusted expected shortfall once from a 10-day shock to all risk factors and multiplies it by $\sqrt{120/10}$, so that every risk factor is treated as having the longest liquidity horizon.
explanation: The FRTB assigns each risk factor its own liquidity horizon through the cascade of nested ES calculations. Scaling everything by the longest horizon would be far more punitive and is not the FRTB method.
originalText: ES is computed once from a 10‑day shock to all risk factors and then multiplied by $\sqrt{120/10}$, so that every risk factor is treated as if it had the longest liquidity horizon.

statement: Under the FRTB standardized approach, liquidity horizons of risk factors are incorporated into market risk capital through the risk weights determined by the Basel Committee.
explanation: The Basel Committee sets the standardized risk weights so that they reflect each risk factor's liquidity horizon: longer horizons lead to larger risk weights.
originalText: Under the standardized approach, the liquidity horizons of risk factors are incorporated into market risk capital calculations through the risk weights determined by the Basel Committee.

statement: The FRTB standardized approach incorporates diversification benefits between risk factors with different liquidity horizons through the risk weights set by the Basel Committee.
explanation: Risk weights reflect liquidity horizons, not diversification. Diversification benefits in the standardized approach come from the prescribed correlation assumptions.
originalText: The standardized approach incorporates the diversification benefits between risk factors with different liquidity horizons through the risk weights set by the Basel Committee.

statement: Under the FRTB historical simulation approach, liquidity-adjusted expected shortfall is estimated by assuming a 10-day liquidity horizon for all risk factors, because their behaviour is highly correlated in volatile markets.
explanation: The liquidity-adjusted ES uses five liquidity horizons (10, 20, 40, 60 and 120 days) in a cascade. A single uniform 10-day horizon is not assumed for every risk factor.
originalText: The historical simulation approach estimates a liquidity‑adjusted ES by assuming a 10‑day liquidity horizon for all risk factors, since their behavior will most likely be highly correlated during volatile market conditions.

statement: Under the FRTB internal models approach, expected shortfall is based on a waterfall (cascade) of liquidity-horizon categories, with each nested ES scaled by the square root of the difference between successive horizon lengths.
explanation: The IMA computes ES from nested 10-day shocks by liquidity-horizon category and combines them using the square root of the differences between successive horizon lengths, assuming behaviour in each further period is independent.
originalText: The expected shortfall is based on a waterfall of the liquidity horizon categories and is then scaled to the square root of the difference in the horizon lengths of the nested risk factors.

statement: Under the FRTB internal models approach, liquidity horizons are brought into expected shortfall through a series of weights together with a correlation factor determined by the Basel Committee.
explanation: The IMA assumes independence across liquidity-horizon categories and uses the square-root rule on incremental horizons. There is no regulatory correlation parameter and no weighting scheme.
originalText: A series of weights is applied to the various liquidity horizons along with a correlation factor determined by the Basel Committee.

statement: The FRTB requires no market risk capital charge for jump-to-default risk, because default exposures are charged only under the credit risk rules of the banking book.
explanation: Jump-to-default risk is explicitly charged within the trading book under market risk capital, through the default risk charge (internal models: 99.9% VaR over one year).
originalText: The FRTB requires no market risk capital charge for jump‑to‑default risk, because default exposures are charged only under the credit risk rules of the banking book.

statement: Under the FRTB, credit spread risk, the risk that a change in the credit spread alters the mark-to-market value of a position, can be addressed within the expected shortfall calculation.
explanation: Credit spread risk is treated like other market risk factors and is captured in the expected shortfall process, with liquidity horizons of 20 to 120 days.
originalText: Credit spread risk, the risk that a change in the credit spread alters mark‑to‑market value, can be addressed within the expected shortfall calculation.

statement: Under the FRTB internal models approach, jump-to-default risk is subject to a capital charge calculated as a 99.9% VaR with a one-year horizon.
explanation: Jump-to-default risk is handled like banking book default risk, with a 99.9% VaR over one year. These numbers are often confused with the 97.5% ES used for market risk factors.
originalText: Jump‑to‑default risk is subject to the incremental default risk (IDR) charge, calculated as a 99.9% VaR with a one‑year horizon.

statement: Under the FRTB internal models approach, the liquidity horizon for credit spreads ranges from 20 to 120 days, and the liquidity horizon for credit spread volatility is 120 days.
explanation: Credit spread liquidity horizons run from 20 days (for example investment-grade sovereigns) to 120 days (other credit spreads), and credit spread volatility has a horizon of 120 days.
originalText: Under the internal models approach, the liquidity horizon for credit spreads ranges from 20 to 120 days, and the liquidity horizon for credit spread volatility is 120 days.

statement: The FRTB backtests value at risk using a one-day horizon.
explanation: Backtesting compares daily P&L with one-day VaR over the most recent 12 months, which gives enough observations for a meaningful exception count.
originalText: One‑day horizon

statement: The FRTB backtests value at risk using a thirty-day horizon.
explanation: A thirty-day horizon would leave too few non-overlapping observations in 12 months. The FRTB backtests one-day VaR.
originalText: Thirty‑day horizon

statement: The FRTB backtests value at risk using a two-day horizon.
explanation: Two days has no basis in the FRTB. Backtesting uses a one-day VaR horizon.
originalText: Two‑day horizon

statement: Instruments in the trading book are marked to market.
explanation: Trading book instruments are periodically marked to market, whereas banking book instruments are not marked to market in the same way.
originalText: Instruments in the trading book

statement: Under the FRTB, trading book instruments are valued using historical cost accounting.
explanation: Trading book instruments are marked to market. Historical cost valuation is associated with the banking book.
originalText: Instruments in the trading book are valued using historical cost accounting

statement: The FRTB distinguishes two types of credit risk exposure to a company: credit spread risk and jump-to-default risk.
explanation: Credit spread risk (a change in the company's spread changes mark-to-market value) is handled with expected shortfall, while jump-to-default risk (the company defaults) has its own default risk charge.
originalText: Credit spread risk and jump‑to‑default risk

statement: The FRTB distinguishes two types of credit risk exposure to a company: credit spread risk and interest rate risk.
explanation: Interest rate risk is a general market risk factor captured in the standard ES. The two credit-specific exposures are credit spread risk and jump-to-default risk.
originalText: Credit spread risk and interest rate risk
correction: The FRTB distinguishes two types of credit risk exposure to a company: credit spread risk and jump-to-default risk.

statement: The FRTB backtests a one-day VaR rather than the stressed ES capital measure, because ES is harder to backtest than VaR and a stressed measure cannot be backtested since stressed data are not expected to recur with the same frequency.
explanation: The capital measure is stressed expected shortfall, which cannot be backtested directly. The FRTB therefore backtests a one-day VaR over the most recent 12 months instead.
originalText: Expected shortfall is harder to backtest than VaR, and a stressed measure cannot be backtested because stressed data are not expected to recur with the same frequency

statement: Value at risk is a coherent risk measure whereas expected shortfall is not.
explanation: It is the other way round: VaR is not subadditive and so is not coherent, while expected shortfall is coherent.
originalText: VaR at the 99% level is a coherent risk measure whereas expected shortfall is not, so only VaR can be validated
correction: Expected shortfall is a coherent risk measure whereas value at risk is not.

changes.from: Value at risk is a coherent risk measure whereas expected shortfall is not
changes.to: Expected shortfall is a coherent risk measure whereas value at risk is not

statement: Under the FRTB, the capital charge for market risk is itself based on a one-day 99% VaR.
explanation: The FRTB capital charge is based on a stressed 97.5% expected shortfall with liquidity horizons of 10 to 120 days. One-day VaR is used only for backtesting.
originalText: The FRTB capital charge is itself based on one‑day 99% VaR, so the same measure must be backtested

statement: Under the FRTB, all risk factors have a one-day liquidity horizon.
explanation: FRTB liquidity horizons range from 10 to 120 days, not one day.
originalText: All risk factors under the FRTB have a one‑day liquidity horizon, so one‑day VaR matches the capital measure

statement: The FRTB tightens the rules separating the trading book from the banking book because banks could lower capital by placing credit-dependent assets in whichever book carried the lower requirement.
explanation: The boundary determines which capital regime applies (market risk versus credit risk rules), creating an incentive for regulatory arbitrage that the FRTB aims to remove.
originalText: Banks could lower capital by placing credit‑dependent assets in whichever book carried the lower requirement

statement: The FRTB backtests one-day value at risk at both the 97.5% and the 99.0% confidence levels.
explanation: Because stressed ES cannot be backtested, the FRTB backtests one-day VaR at both confidence levels over the most recent 12 months.
originalText: One‑day value at risk (VaR) is backtested at both 97.5% and 99.0% confidence levels

statement: FRTB backtesting consists of two tests: a 10-day 99.0% expected shortfall test and a 10-day 99.0% stressed value at risk test.
explanation: Stressed measures are not backtested and the backtesting horizon is one day. The FRTB backtests one-day VaR at the 97.5% and 99.0% confidence levels.
originalText: There are two tests: 10‑day 99.0% expected shortfall and 10‑day 99.0% stressed value at risk (sVaR)

statement: The FRTB establishes a more objective boundary between the trading and banking books, including assignment when a position is initiated and strict limits on subsequent movement between the books.
explanation: The FRTB keeps two books but tightens the boundary with objective criteria, assignment at inception and strict limits on switching, to reduce regulatory arbitrage.
originalText: The FRTB establishes a more objective boundary, including assignment when a position is initiated and strict limits on subsequent movement between the books

statement: The FRTB collapses the banking book and the trading book into a single book.
explanation: The FRTB retains two separate books with different capital frameworks. It tightens the boundary between them rather than merging them.
originalText: The FRTB collapses the banking and trading books into a single book, which solves the regulatory arbitrage problem

statement: Under the FRTB, a sincere intent to trade is necessary and sufficient for a position to be included in the trading book.
explanation: Intent to trade alone is no longer sufficient. The bank must also be able to trade the asset and manage its risks on a trading desk.
originalText: The FRTB says that a sincere ”intent to trade” is necessary and sufficient for trading‑book inclusion; moving a position between books triggers the incremental risk charge as a penalty

statement: The FRTB requires backtesting to be performed on the 97.5% stressed expected shortfall used for the capital charge, with a 10-day horizon.
explanation: The FRTB never backtests the stressed ES capital measure. It backtests a one-day VaR over the most recent 12 months.
originalText: The backtest must be performed on the 97.5% stressed ES used for the capital charge, with a 10‑day horizon

statement: Under the FRTB, stressed expected shortfall measures are not backtested because extreme stressed values may not recur with the same frequency.
explanation: A stressed measure cannot be backtested meaningfully because stressed data are not expected to recur with the same frequency. Expected shortfall is also harder to backtest than VaR.
originalText: Stressed expected shortfall measures are not backtested because extreme stressed values may not recur with the same frequency

statement: FRTB backtesting uses a one-day horizon and the latest 12 months of data.
explanation: The FRTB backtests one-day VaR over the most recent 12 months.
originalText: Backtesting uses a one‑day horizon and the latest 12 months of data

statement: Under FRTB backtesting at the 99% confidence level, more than 12 exceptions in the 12-month period requires the desk to use the standardized approach.
explanation: The thresholds are more than 12 exceptions at the 99% level or more than 30 exceptions at the 97.5% level; breaching either forces the desk onto the standardized approach.
originalText: At the 99% level, more than 12 exceptions in the period requires the standardized approach

statement: The FRTB replaces the incremental risk charge with a default risk charge that recognizes jump-to-default risk and includes equity products.
explanation: The default risk charge explicitly captures jump-to-default risk and, unlike the Basel II.5 incremental risk charge, also covers equity positions.
originalText: The FRTB replaces the IRC with a default risk charge (DRC), which recognizes jump‑to‑default risk and mandates the inclusion of equity products

statement: The FRTB makes no changes to the incremental risk charge introduced under Basel II.5.
explanation: The FRTB replaces the incremental risk charge with a default risk charge (99.9% VaR over one year) that recognizes jump-to-default risk.
originalText: The FRTB makes no changes to the IRC

statement: The default risk charge that replaces the incremental risk charge under the FRTB does not recognize jump-to-default risk and explicitly excludes equity products.
explanation: The default risk charge exists to capture jump-to-default risk, and it includes equity products. The statement reverses both features.
originalText: The FRTB replaces the IRC with a default risk charge (DRC), which does not recognize jump‑to‑default risk and explicitly excludes equity products

statement: Under the FRTB, reclassification of a position between the trading book and the banking book is permitted only in extraordinary circumstances, and any capital benefit from the move is disallowed.
explanation: Transfers are allowed only in extraordinary circumstances such as the closing of a trading desk or a change in accounting standards, and any resulting capital benefit is disallowed, which removes the incentive to switch books.
originalText: Reclassification is permitted only in extraordinary circumstances, and any capital benefit from the move is disallowed.

statement: Under the FRTB, reclassification of a position between the trading book and the banking book is permitted only in extraordinary circumstances, and the bank keeps the full capital benefit of the new category.
explanation: Even when a transfer is allowed in extraordinary circumstances, any capital benefit from moving the position between the books is disallowed.
originalText: Reclassification is permitted only in extraordinary circumstances, and the bank keeps the full capital benefit of the new category.
correction: Under the FRTB, reclassification of a position between the trading book and the banking book is permitted only in extraordinary circumstances, and any capital benefit from the move is disallowed.

changes.from: the bank keeps the full capital benefit of the new category
changes.to: any capital benefit from the move is disallowed

statement: Under the FRTB, reclassification of a position between the trading book and the banking book is never permitted under any circumstances.
explanation: Transfers are allowed in extraordinary circumstances, such as the closing of a trading desk or a change in accounting standards on fair value recognition, but any capital benefit is disallowed.
originalText: Reclassification is never permitted under any circumstances.

statement: Under the FRTB internal models approach, jump-to-default risk has a capital charge based on a 99.9% VaR with a one-year horizon.
explanation: Jump-to-default risk is treated like banking book default risk, using a 99.9% VaR over one year, whereas credit spread risk is handled through expected shortfall.
originalText: Jump‑to‑default risk.

statement: Under the FRTB internal models approach, credit spread risk has a capital charge based on a 99.9% VaR with a one-year horizon.
explanation: Credit spread risk is handled like other market risks, with 97.5% stressed expected shortfall and liquidity horizons of 20 to 120 days. The 99.9% one-year VaR applies to jump-to-default risk.
originalText: Credit spread risk.
correction: Under the FRTB internal models approach, jump-to-default risk has a capital charge based on a 99.9% VaR with a one-year horizon.

statement: Under the FRTB, instruments in the trading book are subject to market risk capital.
explanation: Trading book instruments attract market risk capital, whereas banking book instruments attract credit risk capital.
originalText: Market risk capital

statement: Under the FRTB, instruments in the trading book are subject to credit risk capital.
explanation: Credit risk capital applies to banking book instruments. Trading book instruments are subject to market risk capital.
originalText: Credit risk capital
correction: Under the FRTB, instruments in the trading book are subject to market risk capital.

statement: Under the FRTB, banks must use the standardized approach to compute capital for securitizations such as asset-backed securities and collateralized debt obligations.
explanation: Model-based securitization charges varied widely across banks for the same portfolio, so the FRTB mandates the standardized approach for securitizations.
originalText: The standardized approach.

statement: Under the FRTB, banks may use the internal models approach based on expected shortfall to compute capital for securitizations.
explanation: The internal models approach is not permitted for securitizations under the FRTB, which requires the standardized approach.
originalText: The internal models approach (IMA) using expected shortfall.

statement: Under the FRTB, capital for securitizations is computed with the comprehensive risk measure using the bank's own internal model.
explanation: The comprehensive risk measure was the Basel II.5 internal-model charge. The FRTB replaced it for securitizations with the standardized approach because of the variation in results across banks.
originalText: The comprehensive risk measure (CRM) using the bank’s own internal model.

statement: Under bootstrapped historical simulation, each resample is drawn from the observed data with replacement, the best VaR estimate is the mean of the resample VaRs, and each resample ES is the average of the losses beyond that resample's VaR.
explanation: A bootstrap resamples the existing data set with replacement. Each resample gives a VaR and ES, and the best estimate is the mean of the resample-based estimates.
originalText: Under bootstrapped HS, each resample is drawn from the 500 observations with replacement, the best VaR estimate is the mean of the resample VaRs, and each resample ES is the average of the losses beyond that resample’s VaR.

statement: Under volatility-weighted historical simulation, historical returns are scaled down when the current volatility forecast is above the forecast for the day on which the return was observed.
explanation: Returns are scaled up when current volatility is higher than the volatility forecast at the time of the observation, and scaled down when it is lower. The adjustment multiplies by the ratio of current to historical volatility.
originalText: Under volatility-weighted HS, the −3.0% return enters the adjusted series as −2.25%, because historical returns are scaled down when the current volatility forecast is above the forecast for the day they were observed.
correction: Under volatility-weighted historical simulation, historical returns are scaled up when the current volatility forecast is above the forecast for the day on which the return was observed.

statement: Filtered historical simulation produces VaR and ES estimates that cannot exceed the largest loss in the historical sample.
explanation: Like volatility-weighted historical simulation, filtered historical simulation rescales returns by current volatility and can produce VaR and ES estimates larger than the maximum historical loss. That cap applies to basic historical simulation.
originalText: Under filtered HS, the standardised return of −2.5 is bootstrapped and rescaled by the 1.6% forecast to −4.0%, but the resulting VaR and ES still cannot exceed the largest loss in the historical sample.
correction: Filtered historical simulation can produce VaR and ES estimates that exceed the largest loss in the historical sample.

changes.from: produces VaR and ES estimates that cannot exceed
changes.to: can produce VaR and ES estimates that exceed

statement: The standard bootstrap procedure remains reliable when returns are dependent over time, because each observation is drawn at random from the full window.
explanation: Standard bootstrap procedures presuppose that observations are independent over time. With dependent returns, remedies include bootstrapping GARCH residuals or using block bootstraps.
originalText: Under bootstrapped HS, the standard resampling procedure remains reliable when returns are dependent over time, because each observation is drawn at random from the full window of 500 observations.

statement: Expected shortfall is subadditive, so the combined ES of two portfolios cannot exceed the sum of their stand-alone ESs, and filtered historical simulation can be extended to estimate ES.
explanation: ES is a coherent risk measure and satisfies subadditivity. Filtered historical simulation can be used to estimate ES as well as VaR.
originalText: Because ES is subadditive, the combined ES of the two desks cannot exceed the sum of their stand-alone ESs, and FHS can be extended to estimate ES.

statement: Because VaR is subadditive for skewed loss distributions, the combined 99% VaR of two portfolios cannot exceed the sum of their stand-alone VaRs.
explanation: VaR is subadditive for elliptical distributions such as the normal. Non-subadditivity can occur when portfolios have very skewed loss distributions, so merging skewed portfolios can make combined VaR exceed the sum.
originalText: Because VaR is subadditive for skewed loss distributions, the combined 99% VaR of the two desks cannot exceed the sum of their stand-alone VaRs.

statement: Because expected shortfall averages all tail losses, its estimators have smaller standard errors than VaR estimators, and the advantage grows as tails become heavier.
explanation: ES estimators tend to have bigger standard errors than VaR estimators for heavy-tailed distributions, because ES is more prone to large but infrequent losses.
originalText: Because ES averages all tail losses, its estimators have smaller standard errors than VaR estimators, and the advantage grows as tails become heavier.

statement: Given model risk, choosing the Frechet case for extreme value analysis is the conservative choice, because extreme value risk measures rise with the tail index and wrongly concluding $\xi = 0$ would understate extreme risk.
explanation: One way of choosing between the extreme value cases is to always choose the Frechet, since a test that cannot reject $\xi = 0$ leaves the analyst open to understating extreme risk.
originalText: Given model risk, and since EV risk measures rise with the tail index, the conservative choice is the Frechet case, because wrongly concluding $\xi= 0$ would understate extreme risk.

statement: Because a tail index estimate is not significantly different from zero, adopting the Gumbel case can only overstate, never understate, extreme risk measures.
explanation: Extreme value risk measures rise with the tail index, so wrongly accepting $\xi = 0$ understates extreme risk.
originalText: Because $\xi$ is not significantly different from zero, the Gumbel case should be adopted, since accepting $\xi= 0$ can only overstate, never understate, the extreme risk measures.

statement: If the parent loss distribution is a Student's $t$, the Gumbel case is appropriate because the $t$ lies in the domain of attraction of the Gumbel distribution.
explanation: The Student's $t$ distribution has heavy power-law tails and lies in the domain of attraction of the Frechet distribution, not the Gumbel.
originalText: If the parent loss distribution is believed to be a Student’s $t$, the Gumbel case is appropriate, because the $t$ lies in the domain of attraction of the Gumbel distribution.
correction: If the parent loss distribution is a Student's $t$, the Frechet case is appropriate because the $t$ lies in the domain of attraction of the Frechet distribution.

changes.from: domain of attraction of the Gumbel distribution
changes.to: domain of attraction of the Frechet distribution

statement: The block maxima approach needs no threshold choice but can waste useful data because a block may contain more than one extreme loss, whereas the peaks-over-threshold approach models all losses above a high threshold.
explanation: Block maxima keeps only the largest loss in each block, so extra extreme losses in the same block are discarded. Peaks over threshold uses every loss above the chosen threshold.
originalText: The block maxima approach needs no threshold choice, but it can waste useful data because a quarter may contain more than one extreme loss; the peaks-over-threshold approach models all losses above a high threshold.

statement: The block maxima approach fits a two-parameter generalised Pareto distribution to the largest loss in each block, so it needs fewer parameters than the peaks-over-threshold approach.
explanation: The two-parameter generalised Pareto distribution belongs to peaks over threshold. The GEV distribution fitted to block maxima has three parameters: location, scale and tail index.
originalText: The block maxima approach fits a two-parameter generalised Pareto distribution to the largest loss in each quarter, so it needs fewer parameters than the peaks-over-threshold approach.

statement: A positive tail index places a fitted GEV distribution in the Weibull case with lighter-than-normal tails.
explanation: A positive tail index is the Frechet case, with heavy power-law tails. The Weibull case, with tails lighter than normal, corresponds to a negative tail index.
originalText: A positive tail index places the fitted GEV in the Weibull case with lighter than normal tails, so a positive estimate signals that extreme losses are less likely than under a normal parent.
correction: A negative tail index places a fitted GEV distribution in the Weibull case with lighter-than-normal tails.

statement: Because both block maxima and peaks over threshold rest on extreme value theorems, they remain valid for operational losses pooled across business lines and risk types, whatever mechanism produced each loss.
explanation: Extreme value theory is only valid if a single mechanism is responsible for all observed losses. With losses from different business lines and risk types this is unlikely to hold.
originalText: Because both approaches rest on extreme-value theorems, they remain valid for losses pooled across business lines and risk types, whatever mechanism produced each loss.

statement: The peaks-over-threshold approach models the excess of each loss over a high threshold $u$, conditional on $u$ being exceeded, and does not require the parent loss distribution to be known.
explanation: POT applies extreme value theory to the distribution of excess losses over a threshold. The parent distribution can be any of the commonly used distributions and is usually unknown.
originalText: POT models the excess of each loss over a high threshold $u$, conditional on $u$ being exceeded, and does not require the parent loss distribution to be known.

statement: The peaks-over-threshold approach fits a distribution to the largest loss in each block of equal length, so it uses one observation per block and needs no threshold.
explanation: Using one maximum per block with no threshold describes the block maxima (GEV) approach. POT models all excesses over a high threshold.
originalText: POT fits a distribution to the largest loss in each block of equal length, so it uses one observation per block and needs no threshold.

statement: The peaks-over-threshold approach requires the parent loss distribution to be normal or lognormal, because the excess distribution is derived from the parent's parameters.
explanation: The parent distribution can be almost any common distribution and is usually unknown. The generalised Pareto limit for excesses does not require a normal or lognormal parent.
originalText: POT requires the parent loss distribution to be normal or lognormal, because the excess distribution is derived from the parent’s parameters.

statement: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, $F(u)$ is naturally estimated by the proportion of losses that do not exceed the threshold, because the generalised Pareto fit describes losses only conditional on exceeding $u$.
explanation: The GP fit gives the distribution of excesses over $u$. To obtain the unconditional tail, $F(x) = (1 - F(u))G(x - u) + F(u)$, the share of losses at or below $u$ must be supplied separately from the data.
originalText: 1,940/2,000 = 97%, the share of losses not exceeding $u$, because the GP fit describes losses only conditional on exceeding $u$.

statement: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, the natural estimator of $F(u)$ is the proportion of losses that exceed the threshold.
explanation: The proportion of exceedances estimates $1 - F(u)$. $F(u)$ itself is estimated by the proportion of losses not exceeding the threshold.
originalText: 60/2,000 = 3%, the share of exceedances, because $F (u)$ is the probability that a loss exceeds the threshold.
correction: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, the natural estimator of $F(u)$ is the proportion of losses that do not exceed the threshold.

changes.to: that do not exceed the threshold

statement: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, the threshold $u$ can be estimated by maximum likelihood together with the generalised Pareto parameters, which makes the threshold an objective output of the fit.
explanation: Maximum likelihood estimates $\beta$ and $\xi$ given a threshold. The choice of $u$ remains inevitably arbitrary and judgemental.
originalText: Estimate $u$ by maximum likelihood together with $\beta$ and $\xi$, which makes the threshold an objective output of the fitting procedure.

statement: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, the threshold should be set equal to the target 99.9% VaR so that the generalised Pareto distribution is fitted to exactly the losses that define the VaR.
explanation: A threshold at the 99.9% VaR leaves very few exceedances, too few to estimate the parameters, and is circular because the VaR is the quantity being estimated.
originalText: Set $u$ equal to the target 99.9% VaR, so that the GP distribution is fitted to exactly the 0.1% of losses that define the VaR.

statement: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, the threshold should be set as low as possible, because the GPBdH theorem holds at any threshold once the number of exceedances is large.
explanation: The GPBdH theorem holds as the threshold becomes large. Lowering the threshold to gather more data adds bias.
originalText: Set $u$ as low as possible, because the GPBdH theorem holds at any threshold once the number of exceedances is large.

statement: Lowering the threshold in a peaks-over-threshold analysis increases the number of exceedances and lowers the variance of the estimates, but adds bias because more exceedances come from closer to the centre of the distribution.
explanation: There is a bias-variance trade-off: a lower threshold gives more data and a smaller variance, but the extra observations are less extreme and so the GP approximation is less accurate.
originalText: Lowering $u$ to 1.2% raises the number of exceedances to 150 and lowers the variance of the estimates, but adds bias, because more exceedances come from closer to the centre of the distribution.

statement: Lowering the threshold in a peaks-over-threshold analysis reduces the bias of the estimates but raises their variance, because the additional exceedances come from closer to the centre of the distribution.
explanation: The trade-off runs the other way: more exceedances from nearer the centre lower the variance of the estimates but raise the bias.
originalText: Lowering $u$ to 1.2% reduces the bias of the estimates but raises their variance, because the additional exceedances come from closer to the centre of the distribution.
correction: Lowering the threshold in a peaks-over-threshold analysis raises the bias of the estimates but lowers their variance, because the additional exceedances come from closer to the centre of the distribution.

changes.from: reduces the bias of the estimates but raises their variance
changes.to: raises the bias of the estimates but lowers their variance

statement: Lowering the threshold in a peaks-over-threshold analysis makes the GPBdH approximation more accurate, because the theorem holds for any threshold that leaves many exceedances.
explanation: The GPBdH theorem holds as the threshold gets large, so lowering the threshold weakens the approximation. The number of exceedances is not the condition.
originalText: Lowering $u$ to 1.2% raises the number of exceedances to 150 and also makes the GPBdH approximation more accurate, because the theorem holds for any threshold that leaves many exceedances.

statement: By the GPBdH theorem, excess losses over a sufficiently high threshold converge to a generalised Pareto distribution almost regardless of the parent distribution of the losses.
explanation: This limiting result is why the generalised Pareto distribution is the natural model for excess losses, rather than a normal distribution fitted to the same data.
originalText: By the GPBdH theorem, excess losses over a high threshold converge to a GP distribution almost regardless of the parent, and the GP puts more mass in the tail than the normal does.

statement: By the Fisher-Tippett theorem, excess losses converge to a generalised Pareto distribution only when the parent distribution is normal.
explanation: Fisher-Tippett concerns the distribution of maxima. The GPBdH theorem governs excesses over a threshold and does not require a normal parent.
originalText: By the Fisher-Tippett theorem, excess losses converge to a GP distribution only when the parent is normal, so the GP and the normal give the same tail estimates.

statement: In a peaks-over-threshold model, a fitted generalised Pareto tail index $\xi > 0$ implies a heavy, power-law tail, and the expected shortfall exists provided $\xi < 1$.
explanation: A positive tail index gives a heavy power-law tail. The POT expected shortfall formula, ES = VaR/(1 − $\xi$) + ($\beta - \xi u$)/(1 − $\xi$), requires $\xi < 1$.
originalText: Because $\xi> 0$, the excess losses have a heavy, power-law tail, and the POT expected shortfall exists because $\xi< 1$.

statement: The tail index $\xi$ of the generalised Pareto distribution is specific to that distribution and has no counterpart in extreme value (GEV) theory.
explanation: The tail index $\xi$ in the generalised Pareto distribution is the same tail index as in GEV theory.
originalText: $\xi$ is a tail index specific to the GP distribution with no counterpart in GEV theory, so it cannot be compared with block maxima estimates.

statement: In the generalised Pareto distribution used in peaks over threshold, $\beta$ is a location parameter that measures the central tendency of the excess losses.
explanation: $\beta$ is the scale parameter. The generalised Pareto distribution has a scale parameter and a tail index, and no location parameter.
originalText: $\beta$ is a location parameter that measures the central tendency of the excess losses, so it must be estimated together with $u$.

statement: A negative correlation between the Nikkei 225 and the exchange rate (USD per yen) makes a quanto call on the Nikkei more expensive, because a rising index comes with a falling yen and the seller needs more yen to cover the dollar payoff.
explanation: The quanto seller faces two unknowns: the yen payoff and the exchange rate at which it is converted. A negative correlation between the index and USD per yen makes them move against the seller, so the quanto costs more.
originalText: If the correlation between the Nikkei and $X$ is negative, a rising Nikkei comes with a falling yen, so the seller needs more yen for the dollar payoff and the quanto is more expensive.

statement: The more positive the correlation between the Nikkei 225 and the exchange rate (USD per yen), the more expensive a quanto call on the Nikkei.
explanation: The more positive the correlation, the cheaper the quanto: a rising index comes with a rising yen, so fewer yen are needed to meet the dollar payoff.
originalText: The more positive the correlation between the Nikkei and $X$, the more expensive the quanto call, because the seller must convert a larger yen payoff.
correction: The more positive the correlation between the Nikkei 225 and the exchange rate (USD per yen), the cheaper a quanto call on the Nikkei.

statement: The seller of a quanto call is uncertain only about the exchange rate at maturity, because the foreign-currency payoff it must convert is fixed at inception.
explanation: The foreign-currency payoff is not fixed. It depends on how deep in the money the call finishes, which is why the product is called a quanto (from quantity).
originalText: The seller of the quanto call is uncertain only about the exchange rate at maturity, because the yen payoff it must convert is fixed at inception.

statement: A basket call option on an equally weighted portfolio of two stocks becomes cheaper when the correlation between the stocks falls.
explanation: Lower correlation means more offsetting moves inside the basket, which reduces the basket's volatility and so the value of the call.
originalText: A basket call option on an equally weighted portfolio of the two stocks

statement: A call on the maximum of two stocks becomes cheaper when the correlation between the stocks falls.
explanation: A call on the maximum benefits from dispersion: with lower correlation one stock is more likely to finish high, so its price rises.
originalText: A call on the maximum of the two stocks
correction: A call on the maximum of two stocks becomes more expensive when the correlation between the stocks falls.

statement: A spread call option on the difference between two stocks becomes cheaper when the correlation between the stocks falls.
explanation: A spread option is priced off the volatility of the difference, $\sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2}$, which rises as $\rho$ falls, so the option becomes more expensive.
originalText: A spread call option on the difference between the two stocks
correction: A spread call option on the difference between two stocks becomes more expensive when the correlation between the stocks falls.

statement: Paying the fixed rate in a correlation swap indirectly hedges a stock market sell-off, because correlations between stocks typically rise when stock prices fall.
explanation: The fixed-rate payer is long correlation and receives $N(\rho_{realised} - \rho_{fixed})$, which gains when correlations jump in a downturn.
originalText: Paying the fixed rate in a correlation swap on the fund’s main holdings indirectly hedges a sell-off, because correlations between stocks typically rise when stock prices fall.

statement: Receiving the fixed rate in a correlation swap indirectly hedges a stock market sell-off, because realised correlation falls in a downturn.
explanation: The fixed-rate receiver is short correlation and loses when realised correlation rises, which is what typically happens in a sell-off. The payer is the one hedged.
originalText: Receiving the fixed rate in a correlation swap indirectly hedges a sell-off, because the fund locks in a known correlation while realised correlation falls in a downturn.

statement: Buying put options on individual stocks and selling put options on the index is a way of buying correlation.
explanation: Buying correlation with options means being long index options and short single-stock options, because index volatility rises with correlation. The legs in the statement are reversed.
originalText: Buying put options on the individual stocks and selling put options on the index is a way of buying correlation, because index volatility rises with correlation.

statement: A correlation swap can be valued with standard swap techniques, because traders can bootstrap a market-implied term structure of correlation.
explanation: There is no industry-standard valuation model and no market term structure of correlation. Traders use historical data or stochastic correlation models.
originalText: The swap can be valued with standard swap techniques, because traders can bootstrap a market-implied term structure of correlation.

statement: In 2012 the London Whale sold CDS on the CDX.NA.IG.9 index and bought CDS on individual names, a position expected to profit if volatility and correlation fell in a recovering economy.
explanation: Selling index protection and buying single-name protection is a short-correlation position in credit. In a recovering economy volatility and correlation typically decrease.
originalText: In 2012 the “London Whale” sold CDS on the CDX.NA.IG.9 index and bought CDS on individual names, a position expected to profit if volatility and correlation fell in a recovering economy.

statement: In 2012 the London Whale bought CDS on the CDX.NA.IG.9 index and sold CDS on individual names, a position expected to profit if correlation rose in a recovering economy.
explanation: The trade was the mirror image: index protection was sold and single-name protection bought, with the expectation that correlation would fall.
originalText: In 2012 the “London Whale” bought CDS on the CDX.NA.IG.9 index and sold CDS on individual names, a position expected to profit if correlation rose in a recovering economy.

statement: Correlation swaps are valued with an industry-standard model that discounts the fixed leg off a market term structure of correlation.
explanation: There is no industry-standard valuation model and no market term structure of correlation. Traders rely on historical data or stochastic correlation models.

statement: The present value of a correlation swap rises for the fixed-rate receiver when realised correlation increases during the life of the swap.
explanation: Rising realised correlation raises the value for the fixed-rate payer, who receives realised minus fixed correlation. It lowers the value for the fixed-rate receiver.
correction: The present value of a correlation swap rises for the fixed-rate payer when realised correlation increases during the life of the swap.

statement: For two borrowers that each have a 10% default probability, a default correlation of −0.1 leaves the joint default probability positive, at about 0.1%.
explanation: Joint PD = $\rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y + P_X P_Y = -0.1 \times 0.3 \times 0.3 + 0.01 = 0.1\%$. A slightly negative correlation does not eliminate the joint default.
originalText: With a default correlation of −0.1 the joint default probability is still positive, at about 0.1%, so a slightly negative correlation does not eliminate the worst case.

statement: With any negative default correlation between two borrowers, the joint default probability is zero.
explanation: The joint default probability stays positive until the correlation is sufficiently negative (about −0.111 for two 10% borrowers). Only then does it reach zero.
originalText: With any negative default correlation the joint default probability is zero, so a negatively correlated pair removes the worst case entirely.

statement: With a default correlation of 1, splitting one loan into two equal loans to different borrowers halves the worst-case probability of loss.
explanation: At a correlation of 1 the loans default together or survive together, so the worst-case probability is unchanged and diversification brings no benefit.
originalText: With a default correlation of 1, splitting one loan into these two equal loans halves the worst-case probability from 10% to 5%.

statement: Lending to two borrowers in the same sector reduces concentration risk more than lending across sectors, because intra-sector default correlations are lower.
explanation: Default correlations are higher within a sector, so lending across sectors diversifies more.
correction: Lending across sectors reduces concentration risk more than lending to two borrowers in the same sector, because intra-sector default correlations are higher.

changes.from: Lending to two borrowers in the same sector reduces concentration risk more than lending across sectors
changes.to: Lending across sectors reduces concentration risk more than lending to two borrowers in the same sector

statement: When an arbitrage-free model such as Ho-Lee is fitted to prices distorted by a temporary liquidity effect, such as a forced liquidation, it attributes that liquidity effect to the interest rate process.
explanation: The fitted drift treats the distorted swap prices as fair. The prices are fair given the liquidation, not fair with respect to expected rates and the risk premium.
originalText: Fitting to the distorted prices attributes a liquidity effect to the interest rate process; the 7-year swaps are fair given the liquidation, not fair with respect to expected rates and the risk premium.

statement: Because the Ho-Lee model is arbitrage-free, its recalibrated prices are fair values and its hedges remain accurate by construction.
explanation: Matching market prices does not make them fair values or guarantee accurate hedges. If market prices are distorted, an arbitrage-free model inherits the distortion.
originalText: Because Ho-Lee is arbitrage-free, its recalibrated prices are fair values and its hedges remain accurate by construction.

statement: The Ho-Lee drift can be chosen to match all input spot rates, but the model remains a parallel-shift model with a flat term structure of volatility.
explanation: The time-dependent drift fits the spot rate curve, but volatility is a constant $\sigma$ and shocks move all rates equally.
originalText: The Ho-Lee drift can match all input spot rates, but the model remains a parallel-shift model with a flat term structure of volatility.

statement: Because its drift varies with time, the Ho-Lee model produces a humped term structure of volatility that matches market implied volatilities.
explanation: In Ho-Lee the drift has no effect on the shape of the volatility structure, which is flat. A humped volatility structure is a feature of models such as Gauss+.

statement: Because the drift $\lambda(t)$ is calibrated to market spot rates, the Ho-Lee model rules out negative short-term rates.
explanation: Calibrating the drift fits prices but leaves rates normally distributed, so negative rates remain possible.
originalText: Because $\lambda(t)$ is calibrated to market spot rates, the Ho-Lee model rules out negative short-term rates.

statement: The exponentially decaying volatility in Model 3 introduces mean reversion, so Model 3 is no longer a parallel-shift model.
explanation: Model 3 has time-dependent volatility but no mean reversion, so it remains a parallel-shift model.
originalText: The exponential decay in Model 3’s volatility introduces mean reversion, so Model 3 is no longer a parallel-shift model.

statement: In the CIR model, basis-point volatility rises with the square root of the short rate and falls to zero when the rate is zero, where the drift is positive, which keeps the rate from becoming negative.
explanation: CIR volatility is $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ with mean reversion, so it rises with the rate but less than proportionally and vanishes at a zero rate, where the positive drift pushes the rate back up.
originalText: The CIR model, because its basis-point volatility rises with the square root of the rate and falls to zero at a zero rate, where the drift is positive.

statement: Mean reversion in the Vasicek model prevents the short rate from becoming negative.
explanation: Vasicek has constant basis-point volatility and normally distributed rates, so negative rates remain possible despite mean reversion.
originalText: The Vasicek model, because mean reversion pulls the short rate toward its long-run level and therefore prevents the short rate from becoming negative.

statement: In the Black-Karasinski model, basis-point volatility rises with the square root of the short rate.
explanation: Black-Karasinski is lognormal, so its basis-point volatility is proportional to the rate. The square-root dependence is a CIR property.
originalText: The Black-Karasinski model, because the logarithm of the rate mean-reverts and its basis-point volatility rises with the square root of the rate.

statement: In the Ho-Lee model, fitting the time-dependent drift to market bond prices guarantees that no node of the rate tree becomes negative.
explanation: Ho-Lee rates are normally distributed with constant volatility. Fitting the drift matches bond prices but does not prevent low nodes from going negative.
originalText: The Ho-Lee model, because fitting its time-dependent drift to market bond prices guarantees that no node of the rate tree becomes negative.

statement: In Model 3, $dr = \lambda(t)dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}dw$, the term structure of volatility is flat at any given date, but its level declines over time as $\sigma e^{-\alpha t}$ falls.
explanation: Model 3 changes only the volatility term, which depends on calendar time. At any date all rates still shift in parallel, so volatility is flat across maturities, but the level falls over time.
originalText: At any given date the term structure of volatility is flat, but its level changes over time as $\sigma\text{e}^{-\alpha t}$ declines.

statement: Model 3, $dr = \lambda(t)dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}dw$, produces non-parallel shifts because its volatility decays over time.
explanation: Without mean reversion, shocks move all rates equally. Non-parallel shifts require mean reversion, as in the Vasicek model.
originalText: Because volatility decays over time, a shock to the short rate now moves short-term rates more than long-term rates, so Model 3 produces non-parallel shifts.

statement: In Model 3, $dr = \lambda(t)dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}dw$, basis-point volatility depends on the level of the short rate, which prevents negative rates.
explanation: Model 3 volatility depends on calendar time, not on the level of the rate, and rates remain normally distributed, so negative rates are still possible.
originalText: Because volatility now depends on the level of the short rate, basis-point volatility falls when rates fall, which prevents negative rates.

statement: Setting $\alpha = 0$ turns Model 3, $dr = \lambda(t)dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}dw$, into the Vasicek model with constant volatility.
explanation: With $\alpha = 0$ the volatility is a constant $\sigma$ and the drift is still $\lambda(t)$, which is the Ho-Lee model. Vasicek requires a mean-reverting drift $k(\theta - r)$.
originalText: Setting $\alpha= 0$ turns Model 3 into the Vasicek model with constant volatility.
correction: Setting $\alpha = 0$ turns Model 3, $dr = \lambda(t)dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}dw$, into the Ho-Lee model with constant volatility.

statement: If Model 3 is given an initial volatility and decay rate equal to Vasicek's $\sigma$ and $k$, with a time-dependent drift matching the average Vasicek path, the two models have identical terminal distributions of the short rate, yet Model 3 remains a parallel-shift model while Vasicek does not.
explanation: The terminal standard deviations and means can be matched, so the terminal distributions coincide. Curve dynamics still differ, because only Vasicek has mean reversion and therefore non-parallel shifts.
originalText: The two models produce identical terminal distributions of the short rate, yet Model 3 remains a parallel-shift model while Vasicek does not.

statement: If two short-rate models have identical terminal distributions of the short rate, they imply identical yield curve shifts and therefore identical hedge ratios.
explanation: Identical terminal distributions do not imply identical curve dynamics. For example, a Model 3 can match Vasicek's terminal distribution while shifting in parallel, whereas Vasicek does not.
originalText: Because the terminal distributions are identical, the two models imply identical yield curve shifts and therefore identical hedge ratios.

statement: In Model 3, $dr = \lambda(t)dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}dw$, the standard deviation of the terminal distribution of the short rate declines toward zero as the horizon lengthens, because the instantaneous volatility decays to zero.
explanation: The instantaneous volatility declines, but the terminal standard deviation accumulates the variance of every step from today to $T$, so it can only rise with the horizon (at a decreasing rate).
originalText: It declines toward zero, because the volatility $\sigma\text{e}^{-\alpha t}$ decays to zero.

statement: The Gauss+ model has three state variables but only two sources of risk, because the short-term rate has no random shock of its own.
explanation: The state is described by $r$, $m$ and $l$, but only $dW^1$ and $dW^2$ appear in the dynamics, and $dr$ has no random term.
originalText: The model has three state variables but only two sources of risk, because the short-term rate has no random shock of its own.

statement: The Gauss+ model has three sources of risk, one for each of the short rate, the medium-term factor and the long-term factor.
explanation: There are only two sources of risk. The "+" marks a state variable that is not itself a source of risk, because the short rate has no shock of its own.
originalText: The model has three sources of risk, one for each of $r$, $m$ and $l$, and the “+” in its name refers to this third source.

statement: Rates in the Gauss+ model are lognormally distributed, which keeps the short-term rate above zero at all horizons.
explanation: "Gauss" means rates are normally distributed, so negative rates are possible.
originalText: Rates are lognormally distributed in Gauss+, which keeps the short-term rate above zero at all horizons.

statement: In the Gauss+ model, a larger $\alpha_r$ makes changes in the factors $m$ and $l$ pass into the term structure of rates faster.
explanation: The short rate reverts to $m$ at speed $\alpha_r$. The faster it does so, the sooner changes in $m$ and, through $m$, in $l$ show up in short rates and the whole term structure.
originalText: A larger $\alpha_{r}$ makes changes in the factors $m$ and $l$ make their way into the term structure of rates faster.

statement: In the Gauss+ model, a larger $\alpha_m$ makes $m$ converge to $l$ more slowly and increases the effect of $m$ on longer-term yields.
explanation: A larger $\alpha_m$ means faster convergence of $m$ to $l$ and a smaller effect of $m$ on longer-term yields.
originalText: A larger $\alpha_{m}$ makes $m$ converge to $l$ more slowly and increases the effect of $m$ on longer-term yields.

statement: In the Gauss+ model, a larger $\alpha_l$ lengthens the half-life of the long-term factor, so shocks to $l$ persist longer.
explanation: Half-life is $\ln 2/\alpha_l$, which falls as $\alpha_l$ rises, so shocks to $l$ die out faster.
originalText: A larger $\alpha_{l}$ lengthens the half-life of the long-term factor, so shocks to $l$ persist longer.
correction: In the Gauss+ model, a larger $\alpha_l$ shortens the half-life of the long-term factor, so shocks to $l$ die out faster.

statement: The Vasicek model can reasonably be used to price, compare values and hedge long-term bonds that are first callable after some intermediate number of years.
explanation: Vasicek can be calibrated to match 10- to 30-year noncallable bonds and the 10-year rate volatility, which suits long-term bonds callable after an intermediate period.
originalText: Using Vasicek to price, compare and hedge long-term bonds that are first callable after some intermediate number of years, calibrated to match 10- to 30-year noncallable bonds and the 10-year rate volatility.

statement: Unlike the Vasicek model, the Gauss+ model adds a random shock to the short-term rate.
explanation: The reverse is true: Vasicek has a random shock on the short rate, while Gauss+ is defined by the absence of a shock to the short-term rate.
originalText: Using Gauss+ for caps across the curve because, unlike Vasicek, it adds a random shock to the short-term rate.

statement: For equity options, implied volatility falls as the strike price rises, and when short-dated implied volatilities are historically low, at-the-money implied volatility is expected to increase with option maturity.
explanation: Equity options show a downward-sloping volatility skew in strike. When short-dated volatility is low relative to its long-run level, the ATM volatility term structure is expected to slope upward.
originalText: Implied volatility falls as the strike price rises, and at-the-money implied volatility is expected to increase with option maturity.

statement: For equity options, implied volatility rises as the strike price rises.
explanation: For equity options (stocks and stock indices), implied volatility decreases as the strike price increases.
originalText: Implied volatility rises as the strike price rises, and at-the-money implied volatility is expected to increase with option maturity.
correction: For equity options, implied volatility falls as the strike price rises.

changes.from: rises as the strike price rises
changes.to: falls as the strike price rises

statement: For equity options, implied volatility is lowest at the money and rises toward both lower and higher strikes.
explanation: A U-shaped smile that is lowest at the money describes foreign currency options. Equity options show a downward-sloping skew, with the highest volatilities at low strikes.
originalText: Implied volatility is lowest at the money and rises toward both lower and higher strikes, and at-the-money implied volatility is expected to increase with option maturity.

statement: A European call and put on a non-dividend-paying index with the same strike and maturity gain the same dollar amount in value when implied volatility rises, because $c - p = S_{0} - Ke^{-rT}$ does not depend on volatility.
explanation: By put-call parity the difference between call and put values is independent of volatility, so a change in volatility changes both values by the same amount.
originalText: Both options gain by the same dollar amount, because $c -p = S_{0} -K\text{e}^{-rT}$ does not depend on volatility.

statement: When implied volatility rises, a European call gains value and a European put with the same strike and maturity loses value, because the two have deltas of opposite sign.
explanation: Both options gain when volatility rises (vega is positive for both). The opposite signs belong to delta, which is the sensitivity to the underlying, not to volatility.
originalText: The call gains and the put loses value, because the two options have deltas of opposite sign.

statement: When implied volatility rises, a European call gains more value than a European put with the same strike and maturity, because the call's payoff is unlimited on the upside.
explanation: Put-call parity shows that the call-minus-put difference contains no volatility term, so both options gain by the same dollar amount.
originalText: Both options gain value, but the call gains more because its payoff is unlimited on the upside.

statement: If a European put has a higher implied volatility than a European call with the same strike and maturity on a non-dividend-paying stock, the put is expensive relative to the call, and the arbitrage is to sell the put, buy the call and short the stock, investing the proceeds at the risk-free rate.
explanation: Put-call parity forces a call and a put with the same strike and maturity to share one implied volatility. The option with the higher implied volatility is overpriced, so it is sold and the parity position is completed with the other option and the stock.
originalText: The put is expensive relative to the call, so the trader should sell the put, buy the call and short the stock, investing the proceeds at the risk-free rate.

statement: No action is needed when a call and a put with the same strike and maturity have different implied volatilities, because the equity skew assigns higher implied volatilities to puts than to calls.
explanation: The skew relates implied volatility to the strike, across strikes. At the same strike and maturity, put-call parity requires the call and put to share one implied volatility, so a difference signals an arbitrage.
originalText: No action is needed, because the equity skew assigns higher implied volatilities to puts than to calls.

statement: An arbitrage between a European call and put with the same strike and maturity but different implied volatilities exists only if the stock price is lognormally distributed.
explanation: Put-call parity does not depend on any assumption about the probability distribution of the stock price, so the arbitrage exists whether or not prices are lognormal.
originalText: An arbitrage exists only if the stock price is lognormally distributed, because the implied volatilities come from BSM.

statement: Pricing European index options with a single lognormal volatility equal to the at-the-money implied volatility prices deep out-of-the-money index puts below their market prices, because the implied distribution has a heavier left tail than the lognormal.
explanation: Equity index options show a skew: the implied left tail is heavier than lognormal, so deep out-of-the-money puts trade at higher implied volatilities than the ATM level.
originalText: Deep out-of-the-money index puts are priced below market, because the implied distribution has a heavier left tail than the lognormal.

statement: Pricing European index options with a single lognormal volatility equal to the at-the-money implied volatility prices deep out-of-the-money index calls below their market prices, because the implied distribution has a heavier right tail than the lognormal.
explanation: The implied distribution of an equity index has a less heavy right tail than the lognormal, so deep OTM calls are priced above market by the lognormal model. A heavier right tail is a currency feature.
originalText: Deep out-of-the-money index calls are priced below market, because the implied distribution has a heavier right tail than the lognormal.

statement: If options are priced with a single lognormal volatility, options at every strike are priced at market, because put-call parity forces one implied volatility on every option with the same maturity.
explanation: Put-call parity makes a call and a put with the same strike and maturity share one implied volatility. It does not equalise implied volatilities across strikes, which is why smiles and skews exist.
originalText: Options at every strike are priced at market, because put-call parity forces one implied volatility on every option with the same maturity.

statement: Exchange rate distributions are more peaked and have heavier tails than the lognormal, so deep out-of-the-money calls and puts should trade at higher implied volatilities than at-the-money options.
explanation: Empirically, fewer small moves and more large moves occur than the lognormal predicts. The heavier tails raise the prices of far out-of-the-money options, giving a volatility smile.

statement: Exchange rate distributions have heavier tails than the lognormal only on the downside, so only deep out-of-the-money puts should trade at higher implied volatilities than at-the-money options.
explanation: Foreign currency distributions have heavy tails on both sides, giving a roughly symmetric smile. A heavy downside tail only is the equity pattern.

statement: When a central bank credibly commits to keep an exchange rate within a band, implied volatility is highest at the money and lower for strikes near or beyond the band edges, because the band makes both tails thinner than the lognormal.
explanation: A credible band truncates the distribution, so both tails are much thinner than a lognormal with the same ATM volatility. Options struck near or beyond the band edges are therefore worth less and have lower implied volatility.
originalText: Implied volatility is highest at the money and lower for strikes near or beyond 0.97 and 1.03, because the band makes both tails thinner than the lognormal.

statement: When a central bank credibly commits to keep an exchange rate within a band, implied volatility is flat across strikes, because the band reduces the volatility of the rate by the same amount at every strike.
explanation: A band changes the shape of the distribution, not just its scale, by thinning both tails. Implied volatility therefore cannot be flat across strikes.
originalText: Implied volatility is flat across strikes, because the band reduces the volatility of the rate by the same amount at every strike.
